common_name: Joan Senior Daylily (Classic Near-White Award-Winning Daylily)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans or container divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Joan Senior holds its near-white color best with some afternoon shade in the hottest Gulf South summers, since intense heat can give the petals a faint yellow cast.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch below soil level in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, and water deeply through the first season to establish a strong root system. Bred by Bill Munson and introduced in 1977, Joan Senior bears large, ruffled, near-white flowers with a faint chartreuse-green throat that appear almost luminous in the garden, backed by a light, sweet fragrance uncommon among daylilies. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1994 and remains one of the most widely grown and admired near-white daylily cultivars for its clean color, heavy bud count, and dependable, extended rebloom from late spring into summer. Deadhead spent scapes to keep the planting tidy and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Ruby Stella Daylily (Compact Reblooming Red Daylily)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans or container divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Ruby Stella shares the compact, everblooming habit of the Stella d'Oro line and establishes quickly, often flowering the same season it is planted.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and deadhead spent scapes regularly to keep the near-continuous bloom cycle going strong. Ruby Stella was bred as a red-flowered companion to the famous miniature daylily Stella d'Oro, sharing its compact 12–16 inch height and long, repeat-blooming season but replacing the golden-yellow color with rich, velvety ruby-red flowers with a darker red eye. Like its yellow counterpart, it tolerates heat, humidity, and average soil with ease and blooms from late spring through fall in warm climates, making it a reliable low-growing accent for borders, mass plantings, and mixed containers. Clumps rarely need division more than once every four to five years to stay vigorous.

common_name: Black-Eyed Stella Daylily (Compact Gold Daylily with Maroon Eyezone)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans or container divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; like other Stella-line daylilies, Black-Eyed Stella is fast to establish and forgiving of average garden conditions.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and remove spent scapes at the base regularly to encourage the near-continuous flush of bloom. Black-Eyed Stella is a compact sport in the Stella d'Oro family, producing the same golden-yellow, ruffled flowers but marked with a distinct maroon-red eyezone encircling the throat, giving each bloom noticeably more contrast and depth than the solid-colored original. It shares the same reliable, extended bloom season from late spring through fall, tough constitution, and low, mounding habit that made Stella d'Oro a landscape standard, making it a good choice for gardeners who want the eyezone detail of larger daylily cultivars in a compact, everblooming plant. Divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

common_name: El Desperado Daylily (Yellow Daylily with Red Watermark Eye)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans or container divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; El Desperado is a vigorous, heavy-budded tetraploid daylily that establishes readily and clumps up quickly under good garden conditions.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and provide consistent moisture through the bloom season for the largest, cleanest flowers. Bred by Bill Munson and introduced in 1990, El Desperado bears large, wide-petaled golden-yellow blooms marked with a bold, deep red-maroon watermark eye radiating up each petal from a green throat, a striking color combination that helped it win the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2001. Its high bud count and strong branching produce a long, dependable bloom season, and the tetraploid vigor gives it thick, substantial petals that hold up well in Gulf South heat and humidity. Deadhead spent scapes and divide crowded clumps every three to four years to maintain strong flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Autumn Minaret Daylily (Tall Late-Season Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans or container divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Autumn Minaret's tall flower scapes benefit from a sheltered spot away from strong wind, though the plant itself is otherwise easy-care and long-lived.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving the tall scapes room at the back of a border where their height won't shade shorter neighbors. Bred by Dr. A. B. Stout at the New York Botanical Garden and introduced in 1951, Autumn Minaret sends up remarkably tall, slender flower scapes to 5–6 feet topped with clusters of small, star-shaped, soft golden-yellow blooms with a light spicy fragrance, opening notably late in the season when most daylilies have finished for the year. Its height and late bloom time make it a distinctive vertical accent and a valuable extension of the daylily season into late summer and early fall, when garden color is often waning. Established clumps are long-lived and rarely require division more than once every five or more years.
sources: New York Botanical Garden — Stout daylily breeding records
